explanations.explanation: Baal it is. Jehoram, Ahab's son and king of Israel, removes the sacred pillar of Baal that his father had made (2 Kings 3:2). That's a real step, friend. But the very next verse says he still clung to the sins of Jeroboam. It's like wiping down one counter and leaving flour on every other surface in the kitchen.

Dagon shows up in a different story, where the Philistines have a temple for him (1 Samuel 5:2). Here the text says Jehoram removed the sacred pillar of Baal that his father Ahab had made (2 Kings 3:2). I know, a lot of these old names run together. I mix up my own measuring spoons sometimes, and I have exactly one set.

Chemosh is a good guess, since he's called the god of Moab (1 Kings 11:33). But this verse isn't about Moab's god. Jehoram, the new king of Israel, removes the sacred pillar of Baal that his father Ahab had made (2 Kings 3:2). Same neighborhood of names, different pillar.

Close, but the text says the opposite. Jehoram clung to the sins that Jeroboam had caused Israel to commit, and he did not turn away from them (2 Kings 3:3). Taking down Baal's pillar was one thing, but he held on to these. Think of a man who cleans out the fridge and keeps the mystery container in the back.

Right, he doesn't turn away. The text says he clung to the sins that Jeroboam had caused Israel to commit, and he did not turn away from them (2 Kings 3:3). Clung. That's a tight grip. So even with the pillar of Baal gone, there's still something he won't let go of.

explanations.answer: Rebels against the king of Israel
explanations.explanation: That's it. After Ahab's death, Mesha king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel (2 Kings 3:5). Ahab was Jehoram's father (2 Kings 3:1), and Jehoram is the king who sets out to deal with it (2 Kings 3:6). I'd call that a rough inheritance.

explanations.answer: Doubles what he pays to Israel
explanations.explanation: Doubling it would be a very generous move, friend. But the text says Mesha rebelled against the king of Israel after Ahab died (2 Kings 3:5). Rebelling is the opposite of sending extra. Nobody rebels by sending extra.

explanations.answer: Asks Israel for a new treaty
explanations.explanation: A new treaty would be the polite route. The text takes a different road: after Ahab's death, the king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel (2 Kings 3:5). And Jehoram's next move is to gather an army (2 Kings 3:6).
He does. Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, answers Jehoram, “I will go…” (2 Kings 3:7). He doesn't hem and haw or say he'll check his calendar. He just says yes.

The text says he agrees. Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, replies, “I will go…” (2 Kings 3:7). Jehoram asked for help and he got a yes. If I got that kind of answer when I asked for a hand carrying a mixer, I'd cry.

explanations.answer: By way of the Desert of Edom
explanations.explanation: Yes. The answer is, “By way of the Desert of Edom…” (2 Kings 3:8). The king of Edom joins them too, so there are three kings on this road (2 Kings 3:9). A desert route sounds like a plan that needs a lot of water. Hold that thought.

explanations.answer: By way of the Wilderness of Zin
explanations.explanation: The Wilderness of Zin isn't the answer here, friend. The reply is, “By way of the Desert of Edom…” (2 Kings 3:8). Keep your eye on that desert.

explanations.answer: By way of the Valley of Jezreel
explanations.explanation: A valley sounds nicer than a desert, I'll give you that. But the text says the reply was, “By way of the Desert of Edom…” (2 Kings 3:8). Desert. That word is going to matter very soon.
Water is the missing thing. After a roundabout route of seven days, they had no water for their army or for their animals (2 Kings 3:9). Seven days of traveling and no water. That's a very dry army.

Shelter isn't what the text says is missing. After seven days on the roundabout route, they had no water for their army or for their animals (2 Kings 3:9). The thing that's missing is water, not a roof.

I bet they were tired, friend, but the text doesn't say that. It says that after seven days they had no water for their army or for their animals (2 Kings 3:9). Water is what ran out. A tired army can keep going, but a dry one has a harder time.

explanations.answer: Summoned three kings to hand them to Moab
explanations.explanation: That's what he says. The king of Israel cries, “Alas… for the LORD has summoned these three kings to deliver them into the hand of Moab!” (2 Kings 3:10). That's the king's own take on the situation. Watch what a prophet of the LORD says about it next.

explanations.answer: Promised to send them rain very soon
explanations.explanation: No rain promise comes from the king here. He says, “Alas… for the LORD has summoned these three kings to deliver them into the hand of Moab!” (2 Kings 3:10). He sounds like a man who has already given up. The answer about water does come later, but it comes from somebody else.

explanations.answer: Told them to turn around and go home
explanations.explanation: Turning around would at least be a plan. But the king of Israel says, “Alas… for the LORD has summoned these three kings to deliver them into the hand of Moab!” (2 Kings 3:10). That's a king who sees only trouble ahead. Nobody mentions going home.

A prophet, yes. Jehoshaphat asks, “Is there no prophet of the LORD here? Let us inquire of the LORD through him.” (2 Kings 3:11). He wants to hear from the LORD, not just fret. That's a good thing to ask when the canteens are empty.

A priest is a fair guess, friend. But Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, asks, “Is there no prophet of the LORD here? Let us inquire of the LORD through him.” (2 Kings 3:11). He's looking for someone who can bring a word from the LORD. That's a prophet.

A scribe would be great for writing up the complaint letter. But Jehoshaphat asks, “Is there no prophet of the LORD here? Let us inquire of the LORD through him.” (2 Kings 3:11). He wants to hear from the LORD, not take notes about the trouble.

True. Jehoshaphat says, “The word of the LORD is with him.” (2 Kings 3:12). Elisha son of Shaphat is the man the servant named, who used to pour water on Elijah's hands. After hearing about him, the three kings go down to see him.

The text says he does say it. Jehoshaphat affirms, “The word of the LORD is with him.” (2 Kings 3:12). That's his judgment about Elisha, son of Shaphat. And right after that, the three kings go down to him.

explanations.answer: Go to the prophets of your parents
explanations.explanation: Yep. Elisha says to the king of Israel, “What have we to do with each other? Go to the prophets of your father and of your mother!” (2 Kings 3:13). That's not a warm hello. The king answers, “No, … for it is the LORD who has summoned these three kings to deliver them into the hand of Moab.” (2 Kings 3:13).

explanations.answer: Welcome and tell me what you need
explanations.explanation: Elisha doesn't open with a friendly welcome. He says, “What have we to do with each other? Go to the prophets of your father and of your mother!” (2 Kings 3:13). That's a pretty direct greeting. I've gotten warmer treatment from a locked door.

explanations.answer: Come back and see me tomorrow
explanations.explanation: No appointment is offered. Elisha says to the king of Israel, “What have we to do with each other? Go to the prophets of your father and of your mother!” (2 Kings 3:13). He turns him toward other prophets right there on the spot. Tomorrow doesn't come into it.

explanations.answer: His regard for Jehoshaphat king of Judah
explanations.explanation: That's the reason he gives. Elisha says, “As surely as the LORD of Hosts lives, before whom I stand, were it not for my regard for the presence of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, I would not look at you or acknowledge you.” (2 Kings 3:14). So Jehoshaphat's presence is the reason Elisha names. I'd want Jehoshaphat around too.

explanations.answer: The thirsty soldiers and their animals
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't give that as his reason. Elisha says, “…were it not for my regard for the presence of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, I would not look at you or acknowledge you.” (2 Kings 3:14). The soldiers' thirst is real, but Elisha names Jehoshaphat.

explanations.answer: His respect for Elijah his master
explanations.explanation: Elijah, the prophet the LORD took up to heaven (2 Kings 2:11), is in this chapter, but not in this line. Elisha says, “…were it not for my regard for the presence of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, I would not look at you or acknowledge you.” (2 Kings 3:14). It's Jehoshaphat's presence that earns the hearing.

That's right. While the harpist played, “…the hand of the LORD came upon Elisha” (2 Kings 3:15). Then he speaks the LORD's word to the three kings. I'm no prophet, but I'll say this: a little harp music sounds like a good start.

Sleep sounds nice after a seven day march, but it isn't what the text says. While the harpist played, “…the hand of the LORD came upon Elisha” (2 Kings 3:15). And right after, he's wide awake and speaking.

The text doesn't mention fear for Elisha here. While the harpist played, “…the hand of the LORD came upon Elisha” (2 Kings 3:15). Then he gives the kings the LORD's word. That's a prophet who is ready to speak.

The LORD says the opposite. Elisha tells them, “You will not see wind or rain, but the valley will be filled with water, and you will drink—you and your cattle and your animals.” (2 Kings 3:17). No wind, no rain, and still a full valley. That's a different way to get water than a storm.

False is right. The LORD says, “You will not see wind or rain, but the valley will be filled with water, and you will drink—you and your cattle and your animals.” (2 Kings 3:17). No wind and no rain, and the valley still fills. The animals get a drink too.

Simple is the word. Elisha says, “This is a simple matter in the sight of the LORD, and He will also deliver the Moabites into your hand.” (2 Kings 3:18). Filling a dry valley and handing over an enemy is a simple matter for Him. For me, it's hard enough to get a batch out of the oven on time.

To a thirsty army it might look hard, but that's not what Elisha says. He says, “This is a simple matter in the sight of the LORD, and He will also deliver the Moabites into your hand.” (2 Kings 3:18). Simple, in the sight of the LORD. The dry valley is no trouble for Him.

Costly doesn't show up in the verse. Elisha says, “This is a simple matter in the sight of the LORD, and He will also deliver the Moabites into your hand.” (2 Kings 3:18). Simple is the word he uses. That's a good thing to hear when you're out of water.

explanations.answer: The next morning at the morning sacrifice
explanations.explanation: Yes. The next morning, at the time of the morning sacrifice, water suddenly flowed from the direction of Edom and filled the land (2 Kings 3:20). Suddenly is the word. There's no long wait after the LORD speaks.

explanations.answer: At sunset that very same evening
explanations.explanation: It doesn't come that evening. The text says the next morning, at the time of the morning sacrifice, water suddenly flowed from the direction of Edom and filled the land (2 Kings 3:20). The water waits until the next morning.

explanations.answer: After three long days of waiting
explanations.explanation: Three days would test anybody's patience, friend. But the text says it was the next morning, at the time of the morning sacrifice, that water suddenly flowed from the direction of Edom and filled the land (2 Kings 3:20). That's one night, not three days.

That's it. The sun was shining on the water, and it looked as red as blood to the Moabites across the way (2 Kings 3:22). The text tells us how it looked to them, with the sun shining on it. That's the whole picture they had.

Clear as glass is a nice thought. But the text says that with the sun shining on the water, it looked as red as blood to the Moabites across the way (2 Kings 3:22). What they saw was red, and they exclaimed, “This is blood!” (2 Kings 3:23).

It was morning, and the sun was shining on the water. The text says it looked as red as blood to the Moabites across the way (2 Kings 3:22). Red, not dark. And the Moabites exclaimed, “This is blood!” (2 Kings 3:23).

True. The Moabites exclaim, “This is blood! The kings have clashed swords and slaughtered one another. Now to the plunder, Moab!” (2 Kings 3:23). They saw red water and made up the whole story from it. I think that's a big conclusion to jump to from one look across the way.

The text says they do decide that. The Moabites exclaim, “This is blood! The kings have clashed swords and slaughtered one another. Now to the plunder, Moab!” (2 Kings 3:23). They were certain, and they were wrong about the whole thing.

Not empty. When the Moabites came to the camp of Israel, the Israelites rose up and attacked them, and they fled (2 Kings 3:24). They came for plunder and got a fight instead. That's a rough surprise to walk into.

False is right. When the Moabites came to the camp of Israel, the Israelites rose up and attacked them, and they fled before them (2 Kings 3:24). The camp wasn't empty, because the Israelites rose up. That's a hard welcome for anybody.
Spring is one of the two. Elisha's word included, “…stop up every spring…” (2 Kings 3:19), and the text says the Israelites “…stopped up every spring…” (2 Kings 3:25). Both verses name the spring.

Tree is the other one. Elisha said they would “…cut down every good tree…” (2 Kings 3:19), and the text says the Israelites did (2 Kings 3:25). Spring and tree are the pair that go in these two blanks.

A gate isn't in this list. The text says the Israelites destroyed the cities, threw stones on every good field, stopped up every spring and cut down every good tree (2 Kings 3:25). Gates are never named in that verse. The two blanks are spring and tree.

Towers aren't on the list in the verse. The text says they destroyed the cities, covered every good field with stones, stopped up every spring and cut down every good tree (2 Kings 3:25). The words for the blanks are spring and tree.

No road is mentioned here. The text says they destroyed the cities, put stones on every good field, stopped up every spring and cut down every good tree (2 Kings 3:25). That gives you spring and tree for the blanks.

They don't. The king of Moab took seven hundred swordsmen to break through to the king of Edom, “…but they could not prevail.” (2 Kings 3:26). That was a big push, and it didn't work. So the king is still stuck inside the fight.

False is right. The king of Moab took seven hundred swordsmen to break through to the king of Edom, “…but they could not prevail.” (2 Kings 3:26). Seven hundred swordsmen is a lot of men. It still wasn't enough.

explanations.answer: Withdraw and return to their own land
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. There was great fury against the Israelites, “…so they withdrew and returned to their own land.” (2 Kings 3:27). It's a heavy ending to a heavy scene. The text doesn't say more about the fury than that.

The text doesn't say they take the city. Men with slings had surrounded Kir-haraseth (2 Kings 3:25), but after the great fury against them, the Israelites withdrew and returned to their own land (2 Kings 3:27). So they left instead of staying.

explanations.answer: March on to fight the king of Edom
explanations.explanation: The king of Edom was on Israel's side, one of the three kings who set out together (2 Kings 3:9). The king of Moab was the one trying to break through to him (2 Kings 3:26). After the great fury against the Israelites, they withdrew and returned to their own land (2 Kings 3:27).
